The paper presents an adaptation of Greenberg's potential flow model to predict the loads on vertical-axis wind turbine blades.
The model is extended to handle multi-harmonic oscillations in effective angle of attack and incoming flow velocity, which are more representative of the blade kinematics at low tip-speed ratios.
The static stall angle for the NACA0018 airfoil used in the experiments is 13.1 degrees at a Reynolds number of 50,000.
The turbine blade has a chord of 6 cm and a radius of 15 cm, resulting in a chord-to-diameter ratio of 0.2.
The unsteady blade loads were measured using twenty strain gauges forming five full Wheatstone bridge channels on the blade shaft.

The Greenberg model predicts the radial forces well at the start of the cycle and the maximum force coefficient during the upwind portion, even for the low tip-speed ratio case where dynamic stall occurs.

The Greenberg model deviates from the experimental results once the effective angle of attack exceeds the critical stall angle, and it fails to capture the post-dynamic stall load response during the downwind portion of the cycle.
The Fourier series approximation allows the model to better represent the non-sinusoidal variations in effective angle of attack and flow velocity at low tip-speed ratios.
The experiments were conducted in a recirculating water channel with a test section of 0.6m×0.6m×3m and a maximum flow velocity of 1 m/s.
The experiments were performed at a Reynolds number of 50,000 based on the blade rotational velocity of 0.89 Hz.
The inertial centripetal force of the turbine was quantified by operating the turbine in air and removing the results from the measured signal to obtain the aerodynamic load responses.
The phase-averaged experimental data was presented with a standard deviation band to indicate the cycle-to-cycle variations.
For higher tip-speed ratios (λ=4.5), the Greenberg model predicts the maximum radial load coefficient and its timing well, but fails during the downwind portion of the cycle.
The blade wake interaction, which prevents the build-up of radial force during the downwind portion, is not taken into account in the Greenberg model.

The proposed application of the Greenberg model to vertical-axis wind turbine kinematics shows great potential to diagnose regions of separated flow and quantify the relative influences of dynamic stall and turbine kinematics on the blade loading.
